items.title: Danny Barker — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Can’t get Bobby Johnson. He’s stationed in New York and he don’t want to travel, because he got a hustle in the day with the numbers racket.

ctx.x: You don’t see Cab. Cab is listening. He always had stool pigeons in them big bands. They’re always big-mouth cats in the band, talking about who’s the greatest. The leader don’t have to hear that he is. He hears what the musicians said. Said, “Teddy Bunn’s the greatest guitar player.” “No, Bernard Addison.” “No, Bernard. No, no. Truehart.” “Who’s Truehart?” Say, “Bobby Johnson.” “No, Bill Johnson.” “No, no, man. The greatest is John Truehart with Chick Webb.” So that stays in the leader’s name. So he going to…

got a hustle in the day with the numbers racket. So you . . . here I’m there. I’m ready to jump on anybody. I’ll go with a elephant if the elephant’s . . . [? (inaudible)] a camel. I say, “Let’s go. I’m ready.” Because I done learned . . . I’ve learned to make that dollar and watch that watch. Steele told me. “They would be talking about, I can’t drum. I can drum good as some of these drummers, but they don’t respect me as a drummer. I’ve got to live with that. So you don’t pay what people tell you. If everybody…

items.title: 52115_Danny Barker oral history interview
items.q: And I looked in the big bands, and in Charlie Johnson's band was Bobby Johnson, who was neat, cool, clean, didn't have too much to say, tended to business -- a banjo player.

ctx.x: I found when I got to New York... I looked around and saw all the virtuoso guitar players (there wasn't many [?] banjo players, and they weren't doing much. They were with tramp bands, or they were working in dives and... I saw Banjo Bernie come through, and I saw Speed, Speedy... Speedy worked with Luckey Roberts and them. And I looked in the big bands, and in Charlie Johnson's band was Bobby Johnson, who was neat, cool, clean, didn't have too much to say, tended to business -- a banjo player. There was guys…
There was [John] Truehart in Chick Webb's band, who was the master and the boss of rhythm. Everybody remarked how great he was.
